  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 13 ## Life trials Handling mad people, speaking of madness In this chapter I explain how Qing people interpreted and handled a variety of excessive or abnormal behaviors they called “mad.” I concentrate on three issues in the following order: what acts were seen to deserve that label (more below on terminology), how non-specialists explained the origins of what they called madness, and how relatives of affected people dealt with these afflictions. The last section is a broad survey of the use of the notion of “mucus” in explanations and representations of madness in a variety of late-imperial sources. Since almost all the information presented in this chapter (except for its last section) comes from legal reports, I first explain how the way these reports were produced shaped the information they contained. For one thing, because women committed far fewer “killings because of madness” than men, evidence on the way “mad women” were handled is scanter than comparable information for men. Here and in the next two chapters, I attempt to shed some light on the fears, hopes, and emotional lives of less educated commoners, who usually appear in the historical records only as rebels, criminals, or nameless economic actors. Presenting all these views as representative of “Chinese popular conceptions” would be simplistic. The men and women I discuss lived in different times and provinces, spoke different languages, and were born in different family structures.
